R07-F-01: It is tempting to define kitsch as art that is badly made, but this will not do. Many objects that everyone recognises as kitsch are made with considerable skill: the porcelain shepherdess has been painted with a steady hand, the sunset over the lake is rendered with careful attention to the gradations of orange and violet, and the greeting-card verse scans perfectly. Conversely, a great deal of clumsy work, the amateur's lopsided watercolour or the child's drawing of a house, is not kitsch at all. Whatever makes an object kitsch, then, it is not a lack of craft. A more promising account looks not at the object alone but at the transaction between the object and its viewer. Kitsch offers a feeling that has been decided in advance. The weeping clown, the kitten in a basket, the soldier embracing his mother on a railway platform: each announces the emotion it expects, and the viewer supplies that emotion without needing to look closely at anything. The image functions less as something to be seen than as a switch to be pressed. What is missing is not emotion, of which there is plenty, but resistance: nothing in the work pushes back against the viewer, complicates the feeling, or asks to be noticed for its own sake. A serious painting of grief may also move us to tears, but it usually makes us work for them, by showing grief in a particular face that does not quite match our expectation of what grief looks like. This account explains why kitsch is so often associated with sentimentality, and also why the association is not quite exact. Sentiment as such is not the problem; a good deal of great art is openly sentimental. The problem is sentiment that has been detached from attention, so that the feeling comes first and the object is merely its occasion. The account also explains why kitsch tends to flatter. Because the emotion it calls up is one we already possess and approve of, tenderness towards the innocent or pride in sacrifice, we come away feeling good not about the work but about ourselves. None of this requires us to despise those who enjoy kitsch, or to pretend that we never do. A cheap figurine on a grandmother's shelf may carry real memories, and those memories are not made false by the object's lack of ambition. Comfort is a legitimate thing to want from an object. The danger arises only when the habit of ready-made feeling spreads from the mantelpiece to places where attention matters more: to the way we respond to news of distant suffering, say, or to the way public ceremonies ask us to feel about history. There, the switch that kitsch trains us to press can stand in for the harder work of finding out what actually happened.
R07-F-02: Few rules of modern etiquette are enforced as fiercely as the ban on spoilers. A friend who reveals the ending of a film that you have not yet seen is treated as though he had stolen something from you, and online discussions of new releases now arrive wrapped in warnings. Behind the etiquette lies a theory about what stories are for. On this view, the value of a narrative is concentrated in the not-knowing, and once the outcome is known the thing is used up, like a lottery ticket that has already been scratched. The theory is difficult to square with how people actually behave. Children demand the same bedtime story night after night and object loudly if a single word is changed. Adults rewatch favourite films until they can recite the dialogue, and they reread novels whose endings they could describe in a sentence. Audiences at tragedies drawn from well-known legends have always known that the hero will die; for centuries this knowledge did not stop them from attending, and it may even have been part of the attraction. If knowing the ending destroyed the pleasure, none of this would make sense. What these cases suggest is that suspense is not simply uncertainty about outcome. A viewer can know perfectly well that the hero survives and still grip the arm of the chair when the rope begins to fray, because attention is absorbed in the unfolding moment rather than in a calculation about the final scene. Much of what we enjoy in a story, moreover, lies in the manner of its telling: the rhythm of a scene, the turn of a phrase, the way a minor character reveals himself in a single gesture. None of this is spoiled by a summary of the plot, since a summary is precisely what leaves it out. It would be too much to conclude that spoilers do no harm at all. Some stories are built around a single reversal, and the shock of the first encounter with it is a real pleasure that cannot be had twice; a mystery whose solution has been announced in advance loses something that rereading does not restore. The etiquette, then, protects something genuine. But what it protects is a narrow and unrepeatable pleasure, not the whole value of a story, and a culture that treats the ending as the only thing worth guarding may gradually forget how to enjoy everything that comes before it.
R07-F-03: The phrase 'guilty pleasure' has become one of the most common ways of talking about taste. A person confesses to loving a televised singing contest, a formulaic romance series or a song that dominated the charts in her teens, and the confession is offered with a smile that asks to be forgiven. On the surface the phrase is modest, even self-deprecating; looked at more closely, it does a surprising amount of work, and not all of that work is modest. Consider what the speaker gains. By calling the pleasure guilty, she is able to enjoy the thing while signalling that she knows it is beneath her; she occupies the position of the enthusiast and the position of the critic at once. The confession is a kind of insurance: if her listener turns out to share the enthusiasm, nothing is lost; if the listener sneers, she has already sneered first. What looks like an admission of bad taste is therefore, very often, a display of good taste, since only someone who knows the rankings can confess to violating them. This is why the phrase, for all its apparent humility, tends to preserve the hierarchy it seems to question. Every guilty pleasure implies an innocent one, a set of books, films and songs that may be enjoyed without apology because they are approved. The confession leaves that ranking intact; indeed it needs the ranking in order to mean anything. And the ranking itself is rarely examined. It is striking how often the pleasures labelled guilty are those associated with audiences who have little cultural prestige, the teenage, the provincial, the domestic, while the pleasures of the already respected are seldom described in this way, however predictable they may be. It does not follow that no pleasure should ever make us uneasy. Some enjoyments really do deserve scrutiny: laughter at another person's humiliation, for instance, or the thrill of watching real suffering staged for entertainment. But in those cases the unease concerns what the pleasure does or endorses, not where its object sits in a ranking of prestige, and the honest response is to ask what we are enjoying and why. That question is worth asking of the singing contest as well. Perhaps the answer will be that it offers something real, the spectacle of ordinary people attempting something difficult in public. If so, the pleasure needs no apology; if not, a shrug and a smile will not settle the matter either.
R07-F-04: It is often said that explaining a joke kills it, and anyone who has tried to rescue a failed pun by spelling out its double meaning knows that the saying is true as far as it goes. The listener nods, perhaps smiles politely, but the laugh that should have come does not. The usual inference drawn from this experience is that humour is a fragile, almost mystical thing, which analysis can only damage, and that the serious study of comedy is a contradiction in terms. The experience is real; the inference does not follow from it. Consider why the explanation fails. A joke typically sets up one way of understanding a situation and then, in a single move, reveals that a second way was available all along. The pleasure lies largely in the listener's own discovery of the second meaning, in the sudden reorganisation that happens in his head rather than on the page. Explanation takes this work away from him. It hands over the result without the leap, much as being told the answer to a riddle deprives one of the satisfaction of solving it. The joke is not killed because it has been examined; it is killed because the examination has been done for the listener, before he could do it himself, at the very moment that was meant to be his. Seen in this way, the failure of explained jokes tells us something about humour, namely that it depends on an active contribution from the audience, and this is exactly the kind of thing analysis can discover. There is nothing self-defeating in studying how jokes work, any more than there is in studying how riddles work. The student of comedy who analyses a routine afterwards does not expect to laugh at the analysis; he expects to understand the laugh he has already had. The two activities are simply different, and the second does not undo the first. There is even a case for explanation in the moment, under certain conditions. A joke that turns on an unfamiliar word, a local custom or an allusion to a book the listener has not read cannot produce its leap, because one of the two meanings is not available to him at all. Here a brief explanation does not perform the leap on the listener's behalf; it only supplies the missing ground from which he can make it, and a listener who has been told what the allusion refers to will sometimes laugh a moment later, on his own. The skilled explainer, like the skilled comedian, knows how much to say and when to stop.
R07-F-05: Along many mountain roads there are small paved areas where drivers are invited to stop, and a sign, often bearing the symbol of a camera, announces that a view is available. People get out, look, photograph and drive on. The arrangement seems so natural that its assumptions pass almost unnoticed: that the beauty of a landscape is something seen, that it is best seen from a particular spot, and that the right relation between a person and the land is that of a spectator standing before a picture. These assumptions have a history. The habit of judging terrain by whether it composes well, with a foreground, a middle distance and a far horizon arranged as a painter might arrange them, was cultivated by travellers who had learned to look at scenery through the conventions of landscape painting, and some of them carried tinted mirrors or framing devices so that the real view would more closely resemble a canvas. We no longer carry such devices, but the camera and the viewpoint sign perform much the same function: they select, frame and fix. A landscape that cannot be composed into a pleasing rectangle tends, under this regime, to count as no landscape at all. The costs are not merely aesthetic. Places that photograph poorly, a marsh, a stretch of flat scrub, a slow brown river, are more easily dismissed as empty and therefore more easily drained, cleared or built upon, even when they are richer in life than the dramatic gorge that everyone stops to admire. The spectator's posture, moreover, shrinks what nature has to offer. The smell of wet earth, the sound of insects, the feel of a slope underfoot and the slow change of light over an afternoon cannot be gathered from a lay-by in the two minutes before the engine is restarted, and a beauty that is only looked at from a fixed point is a beauty with most of its dimensions removed. It would be ungrateful to dismiss the viewpoint altogether. For many people a framed view is where an interest in landscape begins; the sign that says 'look here' has taught countless travellers to look at all, and a habit of attention begun at a lay-by can grow into something larger. The trouble lies not in framing as such but in treating the frame as the measure of value. An appreciation of nature adequate to its object would have to include the unspectacular and the unframeable, and it would have to be practised on foot and over time, with the whole body rather than with the eye alone.
R07-F-06: Cuteness is usually treated as the least serious of aesthetic qualities, if it is admitted to be an aesthetic quality at all. It belongs, we suppose, to stickers, toys and advertisements, and a taste for it is regarded as something to grow out of. Yet this dismissal sits oddly with the sheer power of the response. Few experiences in the visual world are as immediate or as hard to resist as the one produced by a large-eyed, round-faced, short-limbed creature stumbling towards us; we feel it before we have decided anything, and it is remarkably similar across cultures that agree on little else in matters of taste. Students of animal behaviour noticed long ago that the features we find cute, a large head relative to the body, big low-set eyes, softness and clumsiness, are the features of the very young, and they proposed that the response is a mechanism for securing care. The explanation is plausible, but it accounts for less than it seems to. It tells us why infants elicit tenderness; it does not tell us why we find the same tenderness stirred by a cartoon kettle with eyes, or why the response is so readily extended to objects that need no care whatever. Once detached from the infant, the cute becomes a style, and a style can be applied to anything. What makes the style interesting is its ambivalence. The cute object presents itself as small, soft and unable to resist, and our response to it is mixed in a way that tenderness towards a real child usually is not. Alongside the wish to protect, there is often a wish to possess and to handle, the half-joking urge to squeeze or pinch what one finds adorable, which people frequently admit to with some embarrassment. The cute flatters our power as much as it summons our care: it is an image of something that will never answer back. This is why cuteness should be taken seriously rather than either indulged or sneered at. A quality that disarms judgement so quickly is a useful instrument for anyone who wishes to make something appear harmless, whether a product, an institution or a mascot standing in for an organisation whose activities are anything but soft. None of this means that delight in a kitten is a moral failing, and the pleasure is, in most of its forms, innocent enough. But an aesthetic that works by making us feel strong and kindly at once, and that does so before thought has begun, is not trivial; its very lightness is what gives it weight.
R07-F-07: The maxim that there is no disputing about taste is usually offered as a courtesy. When two people disagree about a film or a piece of music, one of them, sensing that the conversation is about to turn sour, observes that it is all a matter of taste, and the other, relieved, agrees. The maxim seems to express a modern and admirable humility, for who is anyone to tell another person what to enjoy? But the courtesy rests on a confusion, and the confusion has consequences for the way we talk about art and, in the end, for the way we treat one another. The confusion is between preference and judgement. If you dislike the taste of coriander and I like it, there is nothing for us to argue about. Neither of us thinks the other has missed something; we simply report different reactions, and the reports do not compete, any more than your being cold and my being warm in the same room amounts to a disagreement about the room. Disagreements about novels or buildings are rarely like this. When I say that a novel is sentimental and you say that it is moving, each of us means to be saying something about the book, and each of us expects the other to be able, at least in principle, to recognise it. We point to passages, compare the novel with others, and draw attention to what the other may have overlooked. These are the moves of people who believe there is something to be right about, even if neither of them can prove it. The relativist replies that this behaviour, however common, rests on an illusion. There is no fact about the book's sentimentality independent of readers' reactions, the argument runs, and so our disputes, unlike disputes about the boiling point of water, can never be settled; at most one party tires and gives up. This reply assumes that a dispute is worth having only if it can end in proof. Aesthetic argument, however, does not aim at proof. It aims at a change in perception, and its success is the moment when you look again at the passage I have pointed to and hear the false note I heard, or when I, rereading it at your insistence, find that what I took for manipulation is in fact restraint. Such moments are not rare. Most people can remember a friend, a teacher or a critic who showed them something they had not been able to see, and they do not remember the experience as having been talked into a preference; they remember it as having learned something. It must be granted that some disagreements reach a floor. Two careful readers may agree about every feature of a poem, its rhythm, its imagery, its debts and its departures, and still differ about whether it is good, because one prizes austerity and the other abundance. At this point argument may genuinely run out, and it is sensible to say so. But the floor lies far lower than the maxim implies. Most disputes about taste break off long before they reach it, not because the parties have exhausted their reasons, but because one of them has invoked the maxim in order to end the conversation. There is, finally, something less humble in the maxim than it appears. To tell someone that their view of a novel is merely a matter of taste is to decline to treat it as a view at all, that is, as a claim that might be true and from which one might learn. The maxim protects both parties from the risk of being wrong, but it does so at the price of the possibility of being changed. Real respect for another person's judgement would consist in disputing it.
R07-F-08: When readers began, in large numbers, to write and circulate their own stories about the characters of popular novels and television series, the reaction from some authors was indignation. The characters were theirs, they said; to send them on adventures their creators had never imagined, to pair them with new lovers or to bring the dead back to life was a kind of trespass. Defenders of the practice replied with equal heat that a story, once released into the world, belongs to those who love it, and that the fans who keep a fictional world alive with their own inventions have a better claim to it than the person who merely began it. Both sides, I think, have misdescribed what is at stake. Consider first how unusual the authors' position is, historically speaking. For most of the history of storytelling, retelling was the ordinary way in which stories lived. The same heroes passed from one teller to another, gaining episodes, companions and endings along the way; a poet who took up an old legend was expected to change it, and was admired for the changes. The idea that a fictional person belongs to a single creator, and that others may not set that person in new situations, took shape alongside printing, markets for books and laws that made authorship a form of property. It is not a natural fact about stories, though it now feels like one. Fan writers, from this angle, are less the vandals of a settled order than the late heirs of a much older one. Yet the fans' champions claim too much when they turn this history into a counter-theory of ownership. To say that a story belongs to those who love it is still to speak of belonging, merely moving the title deeds from one party to another. What the older practice suggests is rather that stories are not the sort of thing that is owned in the first place, though particular tellings are. An author can reasonably object to having her text copied and sold under someone else's name, or to having her own work altered and passed off as hers. It is much harder to see what she loses when a reader imagines her characters on another afternoon, so long as no one mistakes that afternoon for one she wrote. The distinction between a text and a world is precisely the one that both sides have blurred. There is an irony here that deserves notice. Fan communities, which began by contesting an author's exclusive authority, have often developed authorities of their own. Long debates arise over what counts as 'canon', over which inventions are faithful and which are betrayals, and newcomers who ignore the accumulated rules can be treated with a severity that few authors would dare to show their readers. In such moments the community reproduces, on a smaller scale, the very proprietary attitude it set out to resist, as though the impulse to fix a story and guard its boundaries were not peculiar to authors but a temptation that comes with loving any story at all. None of this settles every case, and there are surely retellings that wound in ways the distinction does not capture, as when a living author's characters are put to uses she finds degrading. But it does suggest a more useful question than the one with which the quarrel began, which asked whose story it is. The better question is what each kind of claim protects: the integrity of a particular telling, which deserves defence, or the boundaries of an imagined world, which, on the evidence of the long history of storytelling, have never been defensible for long.
